newsitem.title: UK: Council moves to end North Sea oil port blockade.
newsitem.headline: Council moves to end North Sea oil port blockade.

text.p: The Shetland Islands Council said on Monday it will move to end a fishermans' blockade of Britain's key Sullom Voe oil port if they do not move by early Tuesday.

The chief executive of the council Malcolm Green told Reuters that a "special directive" or compulsory order obiliging the fisherman to leave would be issued to ensure the harbour was working on Tuesday morning.
A small group of Shetland Island fishermen took on the might of the international oil industry on Monday in a protest against unpaid compensation claims from the Braer tanker spill four years ago.
At dawn, eleven small shell fishing boats blockaded the strategic Shetland oil port of Sullom Voe in the North Sea, which handles about one-fifth of Britain's oil output.
The Shetland Islands Council own and operate the Sullom Voe port under a speical act of parliament that includes the power to issue a "special directive".
On Tuesday morning a tanker is scheduled to leave the port and another is expected to arrive in the afternoon.

The crews of the boats are protesting against the failure of the International Oil Pollution Compensation Fund (IOPCF) to pay compensation in full for pollution caused to fishing grounds around the islands by oil spilt from the Braer in January 1993.

"(The IOPCF) has consistently denied that any long term damage has been done...But the (fishing) grounds up here are still affected and our livelihood is being destroyed," a fisherman aboard one of the blockading boats told Reuters by mobile telephone.

The blockaders are demanding immediate payment of compensation claims for the past 18 months plus a scientific survey of shellfish stocks to ascertain the level of damage caused by the 85,000 tonne oil spill.
"We will stay until our demands are met or our boats are moved by legal means," said the fisherman who declined to be named.
"The council has every sympathy with the fishermen who are protesting against the IOPC but this is not they way to do it," said Green.
He said a "special directive" meant the fishing boats would have to leave the harbour area or face criminal and civil charges.
If the boats didn't leave it "would become a matter for the police" said Green adding that possible civil penalties might include the cost of delaying huge ocean going oil tankers.
A spokeswoman for the IOPCF -- funded by oil companies and tanker owners -- said that the blockade would not affect compensation claims.
"A number of claims we believe are exaggerated," said Sally Broadley, a claims officer for the IOPCF.

She said that the IOPCF has paid out eight million sterling ($13 million) to the Shetland fishing community, but payments stopped in October 1995 when the limit of compensation for a single claim was reached.
Further claims of 80 million sterling -- of which 22 million sterling is claimed by prawn fishermen -- are now the subject of legal proceedings.

"Our own experts and the Scottish Office have made an assessment of the value of the prawn productivity of the area at 240,000 pounds per year, yet we are being presented with claims of 22 million with little detail to substantiate them," Broadley said.
She said the organisation had no plans for more tests of the area's fishing productivity.
"They're pulling their figures out of thin air...they refuse to take up our offers for a proper scientific survey," said the fisherman.
Sullom Voe is the export terminal for world benchmark North Sea Brent crude, exporting an average of about 480,000 barrels of crude per day.
But oil traders were relaxed about the blockade on Monday with no tankers scheduled to load until Tuesday.

"Sullom Voe is vital to the oil market because Brent is the world benchmark crude. But at the moment it is too early to tell what impact the blockade will have," said oil trader Jim McLaren of Alimar BV in Rotterdam.
